# Global opencode plugins

Plugins here are **machine-level**, not project-level. `agent-harness init`/`update`
never deploy these (they live outside `templates/`); install them into opencode's
global plugin directory with:

```bash
npx opencode-agent-harness install-global        # or: node bin/agent-harness.js install-global
```

That links each `*.ts`/`*.js` here into `~/.config/opencode/plugins/` (a symlink
pointing back at this checkout, or a copy where symlinks are unavailable). Opencode
auto-loads that directory for **every** project and session. Restart opencode after
installing.

## Why global, not a project plugin

Some checks must run even when a project's own harness is stale — and a check
shipped inside that stale harness could never fire, because the stale copy is what
opencode loads. Only a global plugin (plus a global instruction) is
version-independent. See `harness-freshness.ts`.

## `harness-freshness.ts`

On every primary session start it compares the checkout's `.harness.json` version
to the authoritative local harness (`AGENT_HARNESS_HOME`, default
`~/develop/agent-harness`) and keeps the checkout current — **only when that is
safe for the active branch**:

| state | action |
| --- | --- |
| up to date | nothing |
| linked worktree, project **main already latest**, worktree HEAD is an ancestor of main (true fast-forward), no local change overlaps the incoming files | `git merge --ff-only <main>` (never rewrites history) |
| main checkout, no drift | `agent-harness update --target <tree>` (the sanctioned deploy; fails closed on locally-modified harness files) |
| anything else (main stale, branch diverged, overlapping dirty files, merge/rebase in progress, update failed) | **no mutation** — writes `.serve/harness-freshness.json` and injects a session notice so the agent relays it and waits |

A refresh only changes files on disk; opencode loads plugins once at startup, so the
plugin toasts that a **restart** is needed before the updated plugins take effect.

Env knobs: `AGENT_HARNESS_HOME` (authoritative checkout), `AGENT_HARNESS_FRESHNESS=dry`
(detect/report only, never apply).

### Relationship to the manual deploy workflow

The plugin is a **safety net**, not a replacement for the release workflow
(`~/develop/agent-harness/AGENTS.md` step 5: after `update`-ing a project, refresh
its active worktrees). The manual step is deterministic and runs at deploy time; the
plugin only acts at session start and deliberately **blocks** (does not force) the
unsafe cases — a diverged worktree, or a stale project main. Keep both.

# Session handoffs — one file per session

Project-owned (like all `.agents/memory/*`). This directory holds the session
handoff, **sharded**: one file per session instead of a single shared
`handoff.md`. Each concurrent session owns its own file, so two sessions (e.g.
`F-003` and `F-035`) never rewrite each other's "where we stopped" — the failure
mode where one session's wrap-up clobbers another's and its dispatch log is
silently lost.

`npm run test:governance` reads EVERY `.md` file under this directory (plus the
legacy `.agents/memory/handoff.md` if it exists) and requires each to open with a
`## Dispatch log` section containing at least one entry — so a session's dispatch
log is enforced without a shared file. An entry is a bullet line
(`- <subagent> -> <model> -> <shipped/deferred>`) **or** a markdown table data row
(`| subagent | model | shipped/deferred |`); both are accepted, so pick one.
When the log has **5+ entries**, the handoff must also carry a
`## Fan-out justification` section (or a `dispatch_justification:` line) citing
the plan's `§Fan-out review` — the 5–7 band in `orchestration.md` where fan-out
must be justified. That check is forward-only: handoffs dated `2026-09-12` or
later are enforced; undated legacy handoffs are grandfathered.

`npm run report -- --cost` joins the handoff to the observed provider telemetry
via the `session:` metadata line (get the primary orchestrator id from the
`session_info` tool). That join maps a feature to its provider group — the
primary session plus every subagent session it dispatched — so cost per shipped
feature is measured, never estimated. Record it whenever the session did work.
The same join flags a primary session observed on an `escalation_models:` model
(`.agents/memory/model-routing.md`) with no recorded reason: record
`model_escalation_evidence:` (or `none`) whenever the primary ran a pro model.

Mid-session, `scripts/checkpoint.js` (agents: the `checkpoint_write` /
`checkpoint_resume` tools, or `/checkpoint` / `/resume`) maintains a
`## Checkpoint (resume)` block in the session's handoff file. It is
machine-written — replaced in place, never duplicated — and `/resume` prints it
alone as the bounded state a fresh context continues from, instead of replaying
the transcript. Do not hand-edit the block; the handoff's own sections stay
yours.

## Naming & ownership

- One file per session. Name it after the `BACKLOG.md` feature ID (`F-003.md`),
  or a short hyphenated slug of the change (`return-no-condition.md`) when there
  is no feature row.
- **Own your file; never edit another session's file.** That single rule removes
  the collision. To resume a past session, READ its file; to continue the same
  feature in a new session, append a new dated `##`-block — never reorder or
  delete another session's entries.

## Template

    # Where we stopped (handoff) — <feature-id or slug>

    Date: <YYYY-MM-DD>

    ## Dispatch log
    - <subagent → model → shipped/deferred> (empty log = non-compliant session)

    ## Fan-out justification (required when the dispatch log has 5+ entries)
    - <why each dispatch is distinct/necessary — cite the plan's §Fan-out review>

    ## Retries (only when a persona was retried)
    - <persona>: <count> — <what changed on the last retry>

    ## Escalations (only when a persona was escalated)
    - <persona> -> <tier> reason: <evidence> attempt: <n>

    ## Session metadata (structured — record what is known, never fabricate)
    - session: <ses_... — primary orchestrator id from the session_info tool>
    - work_type: <feature|bugfix|investigation|architecture|planning|qa|security|maintenance|process|conversation|other>
    - outcome: <shipped|resolved|deferred|investigation-complete|abandoned|superseded|conversation-only>
    - termination_reason: <gate-pass|checkpoint|blocked|escalated|abandoned|unknown>
    - checkpoint_count: <n> (omit when 0)
    - model_escalation_evidence: <none | persona -> tier: reason> (required when the primary session ran on an escalation_models model; `none` = explicitly no escalation)

    ## Value shipped
    - <1-2 plain sentences: what the user now gets and why it matters — no file paths, no tech jargon>

    ## How (main points)
    - <the key approach in a sentence or two — the "how", not a file manifest>

    ## Done this session (planned → shipped → deferred)
    - <planned → shipped → deferred, one line each, with file + commit refs>

    ## Still open / next
    - <deferred items + next-session entry point>

Lines starting with `#` are ignored by the gate.

# QA plans — one file per change

Project-owned (like all `.agents/memory/*`). This directory holds the
coverage-driven QA plan, **sharded**: one file per shipped change instead of a
single shared `qa-plan.md`. Each concurrent session owns its own file, so two
sessions (e.g. `F-003` and `F-035`) never rewrite each other's entries — the
failure mode where one session's "keep-last-on-top" edit moves another's entry
around (and risks dropping it on commit).

`npm run test:qa-plan` reads EVERY `.md` file under this directory (plus the
legacy `.agents/memory/qa-plan.md` if it exists) and unions their coverage maps,
waivers, and flow audits against the live diff — so a changed code path is
covered if ANY plan file names it.

## Naming & ownership

- One file per change. Name it after the `BACKLOG.md` feature ID (`F-003.md`),
  or a short hyphenated slug of the change (`return-no-condition.md`) when there
  is no feature row.
- **Own your file; never edit another change's file.** That single rule removes
  the collision. If a later change revisits the same feature, append a new
  `##`-block to that feature's file (or open a new dated file) — never reorder
  or delete another entry.
- Authored by `qa-architect` (or by the main orchestrator as the mandatory
  fallback). Required sections: `## Change intent`,
  `## Parallel-surface & variant audit`, `## Coverage map`, `## Waivers`, plus
  the test-design record — `## Test budget`, `## Oracle & owner`,
  `## Test-design self-check` (T1–T10; see
  `.agents/memory/test-design-parameters.md`). The record is what makes test
  quality and economics auditable: coverage without an independent oracle, an
  exit contract, a stated cost, and a wired tier produces suites that are green,
  prove little, and cost a lot.

## Example (`F-003.md`)

    # QA plan — F-003 (return flow: no condition selector)

    ## Change intent
    - change: return flow no longer offers a condition selector — every return POSTs without a condition payload

    ## Parallel-surface & variant audit
    - components/LendingActionDrawers.tsx -> test:quick::return (click-through: Mark as Returned, no condition selector)
    - mobile/features/return/ReturnStatusSheet.tsx audited: deferred — mobile still renders the selector; same simplification pending, logged in handoffs/
    - app/api/transactions/[id]/return/route.ts -> test:api::return (POST without condition payload succeeds)
    - flow: return variant: condition-selector-present audited: removed by this change — asserting absence only

# QA run evidence — one directory per change

Project-owned (like all `.agents/*` data). Full verbatim command/test output for
a QA run lives here, not in the agent's final message:
`.agents/qa-runs/<change-id>/evidence.txt` (same id as the QA plan / handoff —
`F-003`, `return-no-condition`). Only `qa-runner` writes here; never edit another
run's evidence.

Why: the orchestrator's context is the expensive part of a run. `qa-runner`
returns a compact summary (commands + exit codes, pass/fail per suite, evidence
path + sha256) and the unbounded logs stay on disk, so a failure can be audited
without bloating every later dispatch.

Integrity: the runner reports the artifact's sha256 via
`node scripts/qa/hash-file.js .agents/qa-runs/<id>/evidence.txt`; the
orchestrator can recompute it to confirm the summary matches the file.

    # evidence.txt (example)
    $ npm run test:quick
    exit 0 | 42 tests, 42 pass | runner 38.2s, wall 41.0s
    ... full verbatim output, no truncation ...

# Reviews & audits — {{PROJECT_NAME}}

Durable home for **review / audit / investigation deliverables** — the reports a
session produces when it inspects the codebase and files follow-up rows. This
namespace exists so audits stop improvising slugs inside the `.agents/features/`
tree (which is for feature *contracts*: intent → scope → plan → tests) and stop
silently relying on `check-product` treating "no intent.md/plan.md yet" as "not
at planning stage".

## When to write here

A session that runs a code-quality review, regression-package review, logs audit,
dependency audit, or similar **investigation that files follow-up rows** writes
its durable findings here:

```
.agents/reviews/<id-or-slug>/REPORT.md     # the consolidated findings
.agents/reviews/<id-or-slug>/scans/*.md    # per-surface scan output (web/mobile/scripts…)
```

`<id-or-slug>` is the board row ID (e.g. the F-104 code-quality review) or a
hyphenated slug when no row exists yet. One review = one directory; never edit
another review's directory.

## Artifact convention (keep reviews comparable)

Every `REPORT.md` follows the same spine so audits become comparable instead of
bespoke:

1. **Scope + provenance** — what was audited, which surfaces, which session.
2. **Findings, each tagged** with the quality-parameter it violates
   (`.agents/memory/quality-parameters.md`: P1 dead-code · P2 deps · P3
   right-sized · P4 one-home-per-fact · P5 layering · P6 error/state · P7 type
   honesty · P8 consistency) and a `file:line` evidence pointer.
3. **Remediation** — the fix shape for each finding.
4. **Follow-up rows** — every legacy-debt finding that is not fixed in this
   review ships as a board row (evidence cites this `REPORT.md`).
5. **Root-cause findings about the harness** — flag defects in the harness's own
   rules/gates/tools separately, addressed to the harness maintainer.

Reviews that are **no-user-facing** ship as `docs`/`chore`; if the review files
follow-up rows, add a `docs`-type changelog line so the milestone is visible in
the human changelog.

Mechanical quality gates (`.agents/memory/quality-parameters.md` P1/P3/P4) stop
debt from being *introduced* on new/changed code; these reviews clear *legacy*
debt and file the follow-ups.

# BACKLOG — canonical task list

Single source of truth for **all** open work: features, bugs, follow-ups, audits,
roadmaps, ideas. Every other list (`.agents/features/INDEX.md`,
`.agents/memory/todo.md`, historical docs) points here. One row per task — if it's
not a row, it doesn't exist.

**Status ladder:** `backlog → ready → in-progress → testing → shipped → archived`,
plus `frozen` (parked — keep a *why* and a *reopen condition*, never delete).
The board maps status to section: `backlog`/`ready` → **Open**,
`in-progress`/`testing` → **In progress** (active work), `shipped`/`archived` →
**Archive**, `frozen` → **Frozen**. A **Queued** row is a ready-to-pull lane:
`backlog queue <id>` allocates an `Open` row into it, and `/next` (or
`backlog next --take`) pulls the top-priority Queued row into `In progress`.
**Priority (`P`):** `P1` blocking · `P2` important · `P3` nice-to-have · `P4` later.
Priority applies to open/queued rows only. **Evidence** = a pointer
(file/log/ticket/words), never a re-derivation. **Epic** = a declared `## Epics`
key (or `?` when unassigned). **Depends on** = comma-separated row IDs that must
be archived before this row is picked up (`?` when none); `/next`/`take`/`worktree`
skip or refuse a row whose dependencies aren't archived. Leave `?` where unknown —
don't invent.

> Updated in the same session the work happens. Pick up a row by moving it
> `Open`/`Queued` → `In progress`; archive `shipped` rows; freeze don't-delete.
> Historical design docs are aspirational — verify against live code.

# CI/CD pipeline — {{PROJECT_NAME}}

The integration model: **a session lands its gated feature branch directly on
`main` with a fast-forward push; CI gates the landed SHA; the deploy runs only
after CI is green.** There is no pull request, no landing label, and no merge
train — the cycle is deliberately synchronous and simple. A session waits for CI
on the SHA it just landed and is done; the deploy follows automatically.

```
agent worktree (branch)
   │  commit
   │  npm run ship   (rebase on origin/main, branch gates, git push HEAD:main, wait for CI)
   ▼
CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml)                         gates the landed SHA
   ▼
deploy (.github/workflows/deploy-uat.yml)             after CI success: immutable SHA -> prebuilt artifact -> UAT + hygiene
   ▼
UAT health (.github/workflows/uat-health.yml)         scheduled probe
```

A concurrent landing (two sessions pushing around the same time) is normal git
contention: the second `git push HEAD:main` is rejected non-fast-forward, and
`ship` re-fetches, rebases, and retries automatically. The per-feature worktree
(`backlog worktree <id>`) is what keeps two sessions from sharing a checkout.

## What each piece owns

- **`ci.yml`** — the gate on `main`. Runs on every push to `main` (and on a pull
  request if one is ever opened). Extend the `static` job with the harness process
  gates once the harness is CI-installable; enable the DB-backed `runtime` job
  with repository variable `CI_RUNTIME=true`.
- **`deploy-uat.yml`** — triggered by the `CI` workflow completing **successfully**
  on `main` (and by manual dispatch of any ref for rollback). Runs
  `npm run deploy:uat` with `DEPLOY_CI=1`: link from
  `VERCEL_ORG_ID`/`VERCEL_PROJECT_ID`, build once (`vercel build`), ship the
  prebuilt artifact, migrate, seed, alias + commit-parity verify, smoke, hygiene.
  **Fail-closed once configured:** set repository variable
  `UAT_DEPLOY_CONFIGURED=true` and the required secrets; from then on a missing
  secret is a red failure, not a silent skip.
- **`uat-health.yml`** — scheduled probe of `$UAT_ALIAS`; set repository variable
  `UAT_ALIAS`. Every **2 hours** (`0 */2 * * *`) — a sub-minute probe on a tight
  cron is still a *billed* job every run (`*/30` ≈ 1,440 jobs/mo), and
  `npm run test:ci-policy` fails a workflow that reintroduces a sub-hourly cron.
- **`nightly.yml`** — scheduled off-hours E2E (unit/API/routes/browser), **Mon/Wed/Fri**
  (`0 3 * * 1,3,5`), not daily: the push `CI` workflow already runs the same lint +
  quick tier on every landing. The
  heavy device/Maestro tier runs locally via `agent-harness install-nightly`
  (see `docs/nightly-testing.md`); nightly is also where the board is reconciled
  (`reopen` a fix that is still failing, validate one that now passes).

**Cost control.** `CI` sets `cancel-in-progress: true` so a superseded run on the
same ref does not stack billed minutes. Before a cost-visible change (a new
schedule, an expensive runner), run `npm run ci-triage -- --preflight
.github/workflows/<file>.yml` for the dispatch estimate, and `agent-harness
doctor` for the 30-day floor (`ciBudget` in `.harness.json`, when present). The
gate `npm run test:ci-policy` blocks the workflow shapes behind the 2026-10
billing outage; the model is `scripts/qa/ci-usage-lib.js`.

## One-time setup (human-gated)

1. Keep the Vercel Git integration **disconnected** — CLI/CI is the single deploy
   path. Create a token and read `orgId`/`projectId` from `.vercel/project.json`.
2. Repository secrets: `VERCEL_TOKEN`, `VERCEL_ORG_ID`, `VERCEL_PROJECT_ID`,
   `DATABASE_URL_UAT` (optional `DATABASE_URL_UAT_DIRECT`).
3. Repository variables: `UAT_DEPLOY_CONFIGURED=true`, `UAT_ALIAS`,
   `CI_RUNTIME=true` (when the runtime job is validated).
4. Branch protection on `main` (where the plan supports it): allow direct pushes
   (or exempt the landing account), and require the CI check. The harness lands by
   pushing `HEAD:main`, so a rule that forbids direct pushes will reject it.
5. Fill in `.agents/memory/environments.md` with the real dev/uat/prod registry.

## Rollback

Re-deploy a known-good SHA through the same workflow:

```bash
gh workflow run deploy-uat.yml --ref main -f ref=<previous-good-sha>
```

The local `npm run deploy:uat` (with `DEPLOY_CI` unset, from the linked main
checkout) is the emergency path only.

# Gate reference (`npm run <gate>`)

Every harness-shipped gate in one place: what it enforces, how to satisfy it, and
how to waive it. The gates are wired into `package.json` by `init`/`update`
(`HARNESS_SCRIPTS`) and run in the pre-push hook, in `ship`, and in CI. Read this
instead of reverse-engineering the check script — the 2026-09 LibraryOS recon
found `scripts/backlog.js` read 45× and `check-qa-plan.js` 16× for exactly this.

`agent-harness explain <gate>` prints the matching section.

**Choosing a gate:** load the `dev-loop` skill (`skill` tool → `dev-loop`) —
it carries the cheapest-scoped-check rule (`npm run gates -- --phase=quick`),
the project test-tier map in `.agents/memory/dev-loop.md`, and "read the failing
gate, don't re-run it blind". `npm run where` / the `where` tool maps a changed
path to its owning tier.

---

## `test:dispatch` — dispatch-config preflight
`node scripts/qa/check-dispatch-config.js`
Every `.opencode/agents/<name>.md` pins a `model:` that is a real, allow-listed
model (`scripts/qa/models.allowlist.txt`), and every persona referenced by the
rules exists. **Satisfy:** add a persona → give it a valid `model:`; add a model →
its provider to the allowlist. **Waive:** none — a broken dispatch target must not
ship.

## `test:governance` — session-governance gate
`node scripts/qa/governance.js`
Each session handoff opens a `## Dispatch log` (`subagent → model →
shipped/deferred`), and a log with 5+ entries carries a `## Fan-out
justification`. **Satisfy:** fill the handoff's dispatch log. **Waive:** none.

## `test:qa-plan` — diff-coverage gate
`node scripts/qa/check-qa-plan.js [--base=origin/main]`
Every changed code path has a covering assertion or a waiver in the change's
`.agents/qa-plans/<id>.md`, and every touched flow (`.agents/memory/flow-map.md`)
has its sibling surfaces + declared variants addressed in the plan's
`## Parallel-surface & variant audit`. Run scoped: `--base=origin/main` (a bare
`--base=HEAD` is an empty diff). **Satisfy:** author the plan (qa-architect, or the
orchestrator in its place). **Waive:** an explicit `audited:`/waiver line per path.

## `test:backlog` — canonical-single-backlog gate
`node scripts/qa/check-backlog.js`
The shared board service is the only source of truth (ADR 0001); when the service
backend is active the gate validates its board, otherwise it validates the legacy
`BACKLOG.md`. `.agents/features/INDEX.md` and `.agents/memory/todo.md` are
pointers, never duplicate lists. **Satisfy:** edit the board via `backlog_*` /
`node scripts/backlog.js`, never a second list.

## `test:product` — product/UX-first gate
`node scripts/qa/check-product.js`
Feature work has an `intent.md` (Actor(s) → Need → Outcome → Acceptance) and a
value-led `plan.md`; a `plan.md` with no `intent.md` fails. **Satisfy:** dispatch
`product-manager` (intent) → `planner` (plan). **Waive:** non-feature work (no
feature doc tree) is out of scope.

## `test:docs` — documentation hygiene gate
`node scripts/qa/check-docs.js`
No un-substituted `{{PLACEHOLDER}}`, no dangling links, well-formed ADRs, and every
shipped commit is cited in `CHANGELOG.md` by short hash. **Satisfy:** add the
CHANGELOG line in the same commit (a docs-only `chore` commit is not enough).

## `test:concurrency` — cross-session working-tree guard
`node scripts/qa/check-concurrency.js`
Fails when a dirty tree's files are attributed to two In-progress rows that own
the same file (the provable collision), or a tree mixes two sessions' WIP. The
live-session report is advisory. **Satisfy:** `backlog owns <id> --files "glob"`
per row, isolate with `backlog worktree <id>`. **Waive:** `--prune` clears
dead/stale leases.

## `test:integrate` — pre-push rebase check
`node scripts/qa/check-integrate.js`
Fails when the branch is behind its upstream so conflicts surface before push.
**Satisfy:** `git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main` (ship does this).

## `test:quality` — mechanical code-quality gate (NEW/CHANGED code)
`node scripts/qa/check-quality.js [--strict]`
No dead exports / oversized files introduced in NEW or GROWN code (rubric
`.agents/memory/quality-parameters.md` P1/P3/P4). **Satisfy:** extract/split on
growth; leave legacy debt alone.

## `test:wiring` — orphan-test detector
`node scripts/qa/check-test-wiring.js`
Every `*.test.*` / `*.spec.*` file is executed by some package script (T7).
**Satisfy:** wire the test into a tier script.

## `test:linger` — process-vs-tests linger detector
`node scripts/qa/check-linger.js -- <tier command>`
Flags a suite whose process lingers far past its runner-reported test time (an
open handle / teardown bug — T1/T6/T9). **Satisfy:** close pools/sockets/timers.

## `test:capacity` — machine capacity envelope gate
`node scripts/qa/check-capacity.js`
Reports free RAM / swap / PSI load / live serves and fails when the envelope
(`.agents/memory/orchestration.md`) is already exceeded. **Satisfy:** stop idle
serves (`serve.js stop-all`, `prune`).

## `test:ci-policy` — Actions cost-policy gate
`node scripts/qa/check-ci-policy.js`
Fails (or warns) on the workflow *shapes* that quietly leave the GitHub Actions
free tier: a sub-hourly `cron:` (`scheduled-too-frequent`), a macOS/Windows runner
on an unfiltered `push` (`expensive-every-push`), a `-large`/`-xlarge` runner
(`larger-runner`, warn), and two expensive workflows on the same unfiltered push
(`duplicate-expensive-push`). A project with no `.github/workflows` passes.
**Satisfy:** path-filter the expensive workflow (`paths:`), widen the cron to
≥6-hourly, or move it off the push trigger; price a change first with
`npm run ci-triage -- --preflight .github/workflows/<file>.yml`.

## `test:opencode-compat` — OpenCode V2 surface gate
`node scripts/qa/check-opencode-compat.js [--root <dir>] [--json]`
The harness is OpenCode V2-only, so a surface that drifted to V1 is silently
inert. Fails on: a runtime whose major version is not 2 (when `opencode` is on
PATH); `opencode.json` missing/parse-failing or without `experimental.todo:
true`; a leftover V1 config key (`small_model`, `agent`, `permission`, `tools`);
a plugin that imports `@opencode-ai/plugin`, reads `event.properties` (V2 uses
`event.data`), or lacks `export default`; and the V1 layouts `.opencode/tools/*`
or legacy `.opencode/command/`. **Satisfy:** `agent-harness update` (the merge
migrates config, the prune removes the V1 layout) — this is the gate that would
have caught the missing `todowrite` capability. **Waive:** none; a V2-only deploy
is the contract.

## `test:prefix` — cache-prefix stability gate
`node scripts/qa/check-prefix-stability.js`
No volatile value (clock timestamp, machine path, session id) in an always-loaded
prefix file (root dispatcher, rulebook, operating rules, session-start memory).
**Satisfy:** move per-run values into handoffs/state files.

# MCP integrations (project-side, per-agent)

Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers give an agent live external state (the dev
database, a browser, a tracker) through tools. They are powerful and expensive:
**every MCP tool schema is billed on every request that can see it**, and opencode
spawns the server itself — so it bypasses the `serve.js` machine-capacity envelope
and consumes RAM per session. This project wires MCP **project-side, per-agent,
dev-only**. Read this before adding or changing an MCP server.

## The two rules (non-negotiable)

1. **Per agent, never global.** The managed `mcp.use: "*"` policy default-denies
   every MCP server. Append an explicit allow for only the server and agents
   that genuinely need it; re-enable its tools only for that persona.
   An MCP tool the orchestrator never uses is pure context tax.
2. **Development data only.** An MCP server that reaches a database must point at
   the `development` database (`DATABASE_URL`). Never uat/prod — the forward
   boundary in `.agents/memory/environments.md` still applies. Prefer a read-only
   or restricted mode where the server offers one.

## Config shape

`opencode.json` (top level):

```jsonc
{
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "pg": {
        "type": "local",
        "command": ["npx", "-y", "prisma", "mcp"],
        "disabled": false
      }
    }
  },
  // Managed policy denies MCP availability; append this project opt-in.
  "policies": [{ "action": "mcp.use", "resource": "pg", "effect": "allow" }],
  // Deny the server's tools globally (the action prefix is the server
  // name + "_"; V2 permissions replace the V1 top-level `tools` disable).
  "permissions": [{ "action": "pg_*", "resource": "*", "effect": "deny" }],
  "agents": {
    // Re-enable only for the personas that need live DB state (agent rules are
    // appended after global rules, so a later allow wins).
    "data-engineer": { "permissions": [{ "action": "pg_*", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" }] },
    "diagnostics-expert": { "permissions": [{ "action": "pg_*", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" }] }
  }
}
```

- MCP tools are registered **prefixed by the server name** (`pg_*`), so in V2 the
  deny/allow rule is an `action` of `"pg_*"` (the form used above). If action
  wildcards do not match in your V2 build, list per-tool rules instead.
- `--yes`/`-y` on `npx` avoids an interactive install prompt at startup.
- Keep a secret URL out of the tracked config: use `{env:...}` or a local
  untracked override. `npx` servers inherit the project `.env` (dev) as usual.

## Included servers in this project

| Server | Package | Enabled for | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pg` (Prisma/Postgres) | `npx -y prisma mcp` | `data-engineer`, `diagnostics-expert` | schema- and migration-aware; **dev DB only** |
| `playwright` | `npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest --headless` | `qa-runner`, `diagnostics-expert` | interactive web-E2E debugging; run against the `serve.js` dev server |

**GitHub MCP is deliberately not enabled.** It is the most token-heavy server and
is mostly obviated by the direct-land flow (`ship` + `gh` + `wait --ci`). Add it
only on a concrete demonstrated need, per-agent (`devops-engineer`) only.

## Capacity

A local MCP server is a process opencode spawns — it is **not** counted by
`serve.js`. On a small WSL2 VM a heavy server (a browser, an indexer) per parallel
session can exhaust RAM. Prefer remote servers (no local RSS) or one local server
enabled for a single agent. Watch RSS with `node scripts/serve.js list` /
`npm run test:capacity`.

## Verify

```bash
opencode mcp list          # server status + auth
opencode mcp debug <name>  # connection/auth diagnostics
```

## Deploy safety

`agent-harness update` unions managed-first and project-appended `policies`
(duplicate entries are dropped and legacy `experimental.policies` are migrated).
Existing configured servers remain hard-denied after update until the project
appends an `mcp.use` allow; this deliberate breaking behavior is not auto-allowed.
`update` prints a warning naming affected servers, and `doctor` reports each
server with the exact snippet. Sources: `mergeOpencodeJson` / `mergeMcp` in
`bin/agent-harness.js`.

**V1 `tools` gating is migrated, not preserved.** V2 has no top-level or
per-agent `tools` field (only `permissions`), so an older project that gates MCP
the V1 way (`"tools": { "pg*": false }` plus `agents.<name>.tools: { "pg*": true }`)
would otherwise be silently broken: the server reports *connected* while no agent
can call its tools. `update` translates both maps into ordered rules — the
top-level map into global `{ "action": "<name>", "resource": "*", "effect":
"deny" }` rules and each `agents.<name>.tools` map into that agent's own rules
(an `allow` wins the global deny, since agent rules are appended last) — and drops
the V1 `tools` keys. `agent-harness doctor` warns while a project still declares
`tools`; re-run `update` to convert it.

# Mobile / device testing runbook

How an agent boots the Android emulator, installs a build, and runs Maestro
flows **without freezing its own tool call**. The mechanics here are the reason
this doc exists: the naïve way to background the emulator hangs the agent's
`shell` tool forever (no error, no timeout), which looks like "the tests are
taking ages" when in fact nothing is running at all.

## The rule

Any long-lived process — emulator, Metro/dev server, adb server, Maestro driver —
must be launched **detached with its own stdio**, via `scripts/serve.js`:

```bash
node scripts/serve.js start --cmd "<command>" [--url <health url> | --port <n>] [--name <label>] [--timeout <ms>]
node scripts/serve.js list
node scripts/serve.js stop --name <label>
```

`serve.js` spawns with `stdio: "ignore"` in a detached session (POSIX) / its own
hidden console (Windows), records the PID under `.serve/`, and polls the
readiness target with live heartbeats. The tool call returns as soon as the
server is ready.

A **one-shot** heavy command (the APK/Gradle build, a heavy test tier) must run
**capped** too — synchronously, via `run`:

```bash
node scripts/serve.js run --cmd "<one-shot command>" [--name <label>] [--mem-max 3G] [--cpu-max 600%]
```

`run` executes the command in a transient systemd scope with a `MemoryMax`,
streams its output, and returns its exit code; a build that balloons is
OOM-killed inside its own cgroup instead of thrashing the VM. It leaves no
`.serve/` record (there is nothing to stop). An **inline** `./gradlew
assembleRelease` with no cgroup is exactly the 2026-09-30 freeze (Gradle + the
emulator + the dev server filled the 10 GB VM).

## Booting the device tier

**One command brings the whole tier up** (adb server + emulator + app build/install
+ dev server, verified against the health URL), idempotently — reuse it instead of
hand-rolling the ~15 setup calls a device session otherwise needs:

```bash
bash scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/device-up.sh              # full bring-up (reuses what is already up)
bash scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/device-up.sh --no-dev     # emulator + app only
bash scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/device-down.sh            # stop dev server + prune
bash scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/device-down.sh --emulator # also stop the emulator (session end)
```

`device-up.sh` sequences the lower-level primitives, which you can still call
directly. The **adb-server + emulator** primitive brings the adb server up first
(detached via `serve.js`, because a bare `adb devices`/`adb start-server` hangs
forever when the server is down — the forked daemon is reaped with the tool's
process group), then the emulator, then runs a **bounded** readiness gate. It is
safe to re-run — an already-booted emulator and a live adb server are reused — and
it reads the AVD from `scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/local.json` / `MOBILE_E2E_AVD`:

```bash
node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/boot-emulator.sh          # auto-sizes CPU/RAM/GPU to the box
node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/boot-emulator.sh --print-profile   # preview the resolved profile as JSON
```

It expands to (adb server, then emulator, then a bounded gate):

```bash
node scripts/serve.js prune
node scripts/serve.js start --cmd "~/android-sdk/platform-tools/adb -a nodaemon server" \
  --name adb-server --port 5037 --timeout 30000
node scripts/serve.js start --group mobile \
  --cmd "~/android-sdk/emulator/emulator -avd <avd> -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -no-snapshot -cores <n> -memory <mb> -gpu <backend>" \
  --name emulator --port 5554 --timeout 180000
timeout 90 adb wait-for-device
timeout 10 adb shell getprop sys.boot_completed   # must print 1
```

**Right-sizing** (the device tier is the slowest, heaviest part of a run):
`boot-emulator.sh` derives the profile instead of hardcoding it —
`cores = min(AVD hw.cpu.ncore, nproc − reserve)`, guest RAM from the envelope's
`emulator_ram_mb` (the single owner of that number), and the GPU backend is
auto-detected (`host` only when a real renderer answers, else
`swiftshader_indirect`; `-gpu host` on a box whose only renderer is `llvmpipe` is
software GL anyway). Override any of them with `MOBILE_E2E_CORES`,
`MOBILE_E2E_MEMORY`, `MOBILE_E2E_GPU`.

The **display** is a separate latency lever: `MOBILE_E2E_RESOLUTION=WxH` and
`MOBILE_E2E_DENSITY=dpi` are applied after boot with `wm size`/`wm density`
(validated, never interpolated raw into an adb shell). Scale size and density
together — e.g. `720x1600` @ `280` keeps the same dp geometry as the AVD's
`1080x2400` @ `420`, so selectors are unchanged while the emulator moves ~2.3×
fewer pixels per command.

### iOS Simulator (`platform.ios`)

The driver is platform-aware. Select iOS with `MOBILE_E2E_PLATFORM=ios` or
`"platform": "ios"` in `scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/local.json` (env wins; default is
`android`). The iOS route needs **macOS with Xcode command-line tools** — it
cannot boot a Simulator on Linux — and brings up the tier with `xcrun simctl`
instead of adb/emulator:

```bash
node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/ios-simulator-up.sh     # boot/reuse sim + install the unsigned .app
node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/device-up.sh            # platform=ios: skips Gradle/adb, boots sim + dev server
node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/run-maestro.js --flows all --platform ios
node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/ios-simulator-down.sh   # shutdown (add --delete to remove the device)
```

`ios-simulator-up.sh` reads the `ios` block from `local.json` — `bundleId`,
`deviceName`, `deviceType`, `appPath` (the unsigned simulator `.app`) — and emits
`UDID=…` / `BUNDLE_ID=…`; in CI it appends `MOBILE_E2E_IOS_UDID` /
`MOBILE_E2E_IOS_BUNDLE_ID` to `$GITHUB_ENV`. It fails loudly when `xcrun` is
missing (not macOS), the `.app` is absent (build it first with an EAS local
unsigned profile), or no iOS runtime is installed.

`boot-emulator.sh` owns the Android bring-up only: on `platform=ios` it delegates
to `ios-simulator-up.sh`. `device-up.sh` skips the APK/Gradle build, the adb
server, and the adb install/readiness gate on iOS (the `.app` install happens in
the up script), and still starts the dev server in the `mobile` group and gates
on its health URL. `run-maestro.js` resolves the Simulator UDID (explicit
`--udid`, else `MOBILE_E2E_IOS_UDID`, else a booted sim matched to
`ios.deviceName` via `xcrun simctl list devices booted`), skips the adb preflight,
and passes `--device <udid>` to every `maestro test`. `config.yaml` disables
animations on both platforms.

A Simulator has no camera: a camera-based journey (e.g. scan-add) is **not**
covered on iOS — that stays a physical-device check.

```jsonc
// scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/local.json
{
  "platform": "ios",
  "ios": {
    "bundleId": "com.example.app",
    "deviceName": "iOS Simulator",
    "deviceType": "com.apple.CoreSimulator.SimDeviceType.iPhone-15",
    "appPath": "mobile/build/ios-simulator-app.app"
  }
}
```

### GPU acceleration on WSL2 (the biggest wall-clock lever)

On a software renderer the emulator is CPU-bound — ~2.5 s/command, ~3.6 s/tap
(F-291/F-296), pinned near 3 cores just compositing. WSL2 can pass the Windows
GPU through, but Mesa does **not** use it by default, and the DRM node is often
missing too, so `boot-emulator.sh` silently resolves to `swiftshader_indirect`
even on a capable box. Two things are needed, both handled by
`scripts/wsl-gpu.sh`:

1. **Load `vgem`.** Modern WSL kernels (≥ 2.5) ship the DRM module but do not
   auto-load it, so `/dev/dri` is absent and every GL app falls back to
   `llvmpipe` (WSL issues [#12702](https://github.com/microsoft/WSL/issues/12702),
   [#11837](https://github.com/microsoft/WSL/issues/11837)).
2. **Select the `d3d12` driver.** Even with `/dev/dri` present, Mesa still picks
   `llvmpipe` unless `GALLIUM_DRIVER=d3d12` (with `/usr/lib/wsl/lib` on the
   loader path) is set.

```bash
bash scripts/wsl-gpu.sh status    # diagnose: /dev/dxg, vgem, d3d12 renderer
bash scripts/wsl-gpu.sh apply     # load + persist vgem, verify d3d12 (auto-sudo)
```

Once active, `glxinfo -B` reports `D3D12 (<Windows GPU>)` and `Accelerated: yes`,
and `boot-emulator.sh --print-profile` resolves `gpu: "host"` with a `gpuEnv`
that exports the two variables to the emulator (serve.js forwards the caller's
env), plus a `gpuExtra` of `-feature -Vulkan`. **Vulkan must be disabled on this
path**: the emulator's gfxstream Vulkan backend segfaults qemu mid-boot under
Mesa `d3d12` (the `Segmentation fault (core dumped)` that made every F-296 run
fall back to the software rasterizer), while GLES-over-`host` on d3d12 is stable
and hardware-accelerated. Verified on this box: `-gpu host -feature -Vulkan`
boots to `D3D12 (Intel(R) Graphics)` in ~20 s; `-gpu host` without it crashes. Verification on this box: before — `llvmpipe`, `Accelerated: no`; after —
`D3D12 (Intel(R) Graphics)`, `Accelerated: yes`. The script is a no-op outside
WSL (no `/dev/dxg`). The Huawei/Xiaomi/etc. GPU must have a WSL-capable driver
(the Intel/AMD/NVIDIA "WSL" driver); if `apply` loads `vgem` but d3d12 still
reports software, `wsl --shutdown` from Windows and retry.

The emulator joins the machine-wide **`mobile` tier group** (`--group mobile`):
the emulator and the dev server are two heavy processes that legitimately run
together for device E2E, so they share ONE budgeted tier instead of tripping the
single-heavy-tier lock. Start the dev server in the same group (see below). A
third, unrelated heavy tier is still refused.

The group shares ONE **combined** memory budget (`group_mem_max_mb`, default 7 GB):
each member's per-process cap is generous (a 2048 MB AVD peaks ~4.4 GB RSS), so
`serve.js` tightens a new member to the group's remaining budget instead of letting
emulator + dev server each take 5 GB and fill the VM. An explicit `--mem-max` wins;
a near-exhausted budget refuses (`--force` overrides).

**Both members set an explicit `--mem-max`** (the group budget sums *caps*, not
usage, so leaving them implicit lets the first-started member claim the full
`heavy_mem_max_mb` and tightens the second to the tiny remainder — which pinned
the emulator at exactly its guest RAM, ~95 k reclaim events):

| Member | Cap | Override |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dev server (`next dev`) | `2560 MB` | `MOBILE_E2E_DEV_MEM_MAX` |
| emulator (`qemu`) | `guest RAM + 2048 MB` | `MOBILE_E2E_MEM_MAX` |

Keep `devCap + emuCap ≤ group_mem_max_mb` (2560 + 4096 = 6656 ≤ 7168). If you
raise `emulator_ram_mb`, the emulator cap scales with it and you may need to raise
`group_mem_max_mb` too; on a software renderer (`swiftshader_indirect`) set
`MOBILE_E2E_MEM_MAX` higher, since QEMU's RSS there is well above guest RAM.

#### Optional: run the backend as a production server

`next dev` compiles on demand and swings up to ~1.9 GB, competing with the
emulator for the shared group budget. A production backend (`next build` once,
then `next start`) is far leaner and steadier across the long matrix run. Opt in
per project in `local.json`:

```json
{
  "devCmd": "npm run start",
  "devBuildCmd": "npm run build",
  "devBuildCache": ["app/**", "lib/**", "next.config.*", "package.json"],
  "devBuildOutput": ".next/BUILD_ID"
}
```

When `devBuildCmd` is set, `device-up.sh` runs it as a **capped one-shot**
(`serve.js run`, group `mobile`) after the APK build and before the emulator, so
two heavy one-shots never overlap; a failed build aborts the bring-up. The
`devBuildCache` globs are resolved through `git ls-files` (so `node_modules`/
`.next` never enter the hash) and `backend-build-cache.js` skips the build when
nothing under them changed **and** `devBuildOutput` (when declared) still exists
— a deleted build is a miss, never a skip that leaves `next start` with nothing.
Force a rebuild with `MOBILE_E2E_DEV_BUILD_FORCE=1`;
override the command with `MOBILE_E2E_DEV_BUILD_CMD`. With no `devBuildCmd` the
behavior is unchanged (`npm run dev`, no build).

### Building the APK (always capped)

`scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/build-apk.sh` builds the release APK: it runs `expo prebuild`
only when `mobile/android/` is absent, patches `usesCleartextTraffic` into the
generated manifest, right-sizes Gradle (no daemon, one worker, one ABI, 1 GB heap),
and runs `assembleRelease` through `serve.js run` (default `mem≤3G`). Run the
build BEFORE the dev server is up, and never call `./gradlew assembleRelease`
inline — that is the 2026-09-30 freeze. `device-up.sh` calls it automatically:

Every adb call is `timeout`-wrapped: a wedged adb fails fast instead of hanging
the tool. `run-maestro.js` also preflights adb (10 s probe) and exits with the
exact recovery step rather than blocking. `serve.js list`/`start` auto-prune dead
`.serve/` records, so a stale adb-server/emulator entry from a killed session
cannot misreport the machine.

On Linux with a systemd user bus, `--mem-max`/`--cpu-max` put the emulator in
its own cgroup: if it runs away it is throttled or OOM-killed *inside the unit*
rather than dragging the whole WSL VM into swap-thrash. They are ignored with a
warning elsewhere.

- **Size it to the box.** The emulator is a heavy tier: software rendering
  (`-gpu swiftshader_indirect`) pins a core and *still* used ~3 GB in the
  2026-09-29 freeze (QEMU + software-GPU overhead far above `hw.ramSize`) — the
  observed QEMU RSS at a 2048 MB guest is ~4.4 GB. `boot-emulator.sh` right-sizes
  cores to the host (a fixed 2 cores made QEMU the bottleneck on an 8-vCPU box),
  reads guest RAM from the envelope, and picks the GPU backend automatically.
  The emulator's own cgroup cap defaults to `emulator_ram_mb` + ~2 GB
  (`MOBILE_E2E_MEM_MAX`), leaving room for QEMU's host-side overhead and page
  cache instead of pinning it at guest RAM. `serve.js` refuses a heavy launch that would
  exceed the capacity envelope (`.agents/memory/orchestration.md`) — stop another
  tier first, or `--force` to override deliberately.
- The SDK path and AVD name are per-project. On WSL2 the active AVD is
  `libraryos`. The emulator exposes the adb port at **5554**, which is what
  `--port` probes.
- A full cold boot takes ~30 s; `--timeout 120000` gives headroom. A start
  prints a "launching" line up front, so an in-progress wait is never silent.
- On a systemd-less WSL there is no `/run/user/<uid>`; the emulator aborts
  (`Aborted (core dumped)`) without a writable `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`. `boot-emulator.sh`
  resolves a private temp runtime dir automatically, so this is not a manual step.
- The dev server is a **separate** detached process, but part of the same device
  tier — start it in the **same group** so the pair is budgeted as one:
  `node scripts/serve.js start --cmd "npm run dev" --url http://localhost:3000 --name app-dev --group mobile`.

### Startup speed: content-addressed APK cache + quickboot

The cold `assembleRelease` dominates the tier (7-11 min on a fresh worktree; the
reanimated/worklets C++ compile, new-arch codegen, and dex merge are the cost).
Almost all of it is invariant across worktrees for a fixed dependency set — only
the JS bundle changes. `scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/apk-cache.js` content-addresses each
stage so the invariant work is done once:

```
~/.cache/agent-harness/mobile-e2e/
├── native/<nativeKey>/base.apk      native shell  (deps/toolchain; ignores JS)
├── bundle/<bundleKey>/              Hermes bundle + exported assets (JS sources)
└── apk/<fullKey>/app-release.apk    ready-to-install APK (native + JS)
```

`build-apk.sh` (and therefore `device-up.sh`) tries, in order: **full-key hit →
overlay → full build**. The overlay re-bundles only JS, drops it into the cached
native base, and re-signs with the app's debug keystore (`zipalign` +
`apksigner`); it never touches `resources.arsc`, and it declines (falling back to
Gradle) if the bundle references an asset the base lacks or if any verify step
fails. It is a pure accelerator — correctness never depends on it. Measured on
LibraryOS: **~7 s warm / ~20-30 s cold** for the overlay versus minutes for a
cold build.

| env | default | effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MOBILE_E2E_SKIP_CACHE` | `0` | `1` bypasses the cache entirely |
| `MOBILE_E2E_APK_OVERLAY` | `1` | `0` disables the overlay (full build on JS change) |
| `MOBILE_E2E_SNAPSHOT` | `1` | `0` disables the emulator quickboot snapshot |
| `MOBILE_E2E_SNAPSHOT_NAME` | `agent-e2e` | snapshot name |
| `MOBILE_E2E_OVERLAP` | `1` | `0` starts the dev server after the boot, not with it |

- **Gradle reuse.** The managed `gradle.properties` block now enables
  `org.gradle.caching` (shared local cache in `~/.gradle`) and the configuration
  cache, and the assemble runs with `--build-cache --configuration-cache`, so a
  fresh worktree reuses invariant task outputs instead of recompiling.
- **Prewarm off the critical path.** `scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/prewarm.sh` warms the
  cache (hit/overlay/build, capped) and is idempotent; `prewarm.sh --detach`
  runs it in the background. Set `AGENT_HARNESS_PREWARM=1` to have
  `agent-harness update` launch it automatically. It obeys the capacity envelope
  (`prewarm.sh` classifies as an "apk build" one-shot), so it refuses when a
  heavy tier is live rather than thrashing the VM.
- **Quickboot snapshot.** `boot-emulator.sh` boots with `-snapshot agent-e2e`
  when enabled, so a warm snapshot turns the ~24-31 s cold boot into seconds.
  This VHD/AVD keeps its data in a qcow2 overlay and the emulator ships with
  `Feature QuickbootFileBacked` **off** ("disabled due to stability issues"), so
  a snapshot save/load silently fails (`Device 'cache' does not have the
  requested snapshot`) and every bring-up cold-boots. `boot-emulator.sh` now
  forces `ANDROID_EMU_FORCE_QUICKBOOT_FILE_BACKED=1`, which is what makes it
  actually work — measured **9 s wall-clock / ~4 s to restore** vs 24-31 s cold
  on this box. An incomplete save (a stray `snapshot.pb` with no `ram.bin`) is
  discarded up front. Because a snapshot is stateful, a failed boot retries once
  **cold** before the GPU fallback; `device-down.sh --emulator` saves the
  snapshot before stopping and reports a save failure to
  `.serve/snapshot-save.log` instead of swallowing it. Disable it entirely with
  `MOBILE_E2E_SNAPSHOT=0` if quickboot ever proves unstable.
- **Overlap.** The dev-server start (independent of the device) runs
  concurrently with the emulator boot; the install joins both. `device-up.sh`
  prints `device-up:timings {…}` per phase and appends it to
  `.serve/device-up-timings.jsonl`.

### Readiness gate (never `sleep`-and-pray)

```bash
adb wait-for-device
adb shell getprop sys.boot_completed   # must print 1
```

Only then `adb install -r <apk>` and run flows. Both are synchronous one-shots —
run them inline and let output stream; never pipe a run through a buffering
filter (`| tail`, redirect-to-file-then-read), or it looks frozen and gets
aborted mid-flight.

## Making a full run fast and observable

A full multi-journey Maestro matrix on a software-rendered emulator can take tens
of minutes. The runner (`scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/run-maestro.js`, harness-owned)
carries a performance layer; coverage and assertions are unchanged:

1. **Launch detached, then get notified — do NOT sleep/poll.** Never block the
   tool for the whole run, and never guess a finish time with `sleep N; grep`.
   The helper runs the matrix with its own session/stdio and writes a
   machine-readable job:

   ```bash
   scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/run-detached.sh --flows all --reuse-session
   ```

   It writes `<jobdir>/<id>.events.jsonl` (one JSON line per scenario: start,
   pass/fail, fail-fast, done, with `durationMs`) plus `<jobdir>/<id>.json`
   (pid + log + events paths). The `job-notify` opencode plugin tails the stream
   and turns it into a **push**: a console-log line per scenario (V2 server
   plugins have no TUI toast; live progress with no LLM turn), and a message
   injected back into the session (`session.prompt`) on the **first failure** and
   at **completion** — so the agent resumes on real results instead of polling.
   The report lands at `.serve/mobile-e2e-last-run.json` and now carries the
   **invocation count, matrix/invocation wall time, and each
   journey's `durationMs`** (parsed from Maestro's per-flow summary in a batch,
   or the invocation wall clock for a single flow), plus a `Slowest journeys:`
    line — the timing map H-34 asked for. A batched failure is matched by its
    extension-free flow key, so it can never be silently reported as a pass (the
    2026-10-01 run lost 2 of its 3 failures that way).

    **`analyze-timings.js`** is the per-command ruler for the optimization loop.
    It parses each invocation's `~/.maestro/tests/<run>/maestro.log` and reports
    per-kind latency plus **dead waits** — an `(Optional)` command that ends
    WARNED, i.e. burned its whole timeout doing nothing (the 2026-10-02 matrix
    lost 7.4 min to a single re-expiring `dashboard-profile-button` wait):

    ```bash
    node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/analyze-timings.js --prefix 2026-10-02_
    node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/analyze-timings.js --dir ~/.maestro/tests/2026-10-02_080659 --json
    ```

   **To block for the run's exit code, prefer the async `wait` TOOL, not a
   `--wait` shell call.** The general `wait` tool (`scripts/wait-for.js`, e.g.
   `wait --job <record.json>`) spawns its child asynchronously, so it does
   **not** freeze opencode's event loop — the plugin's log lines and
   first-failure/completion wakes keep flowing while the agent waits. (Before
   0.1.115 the `wait` tool used `execFileSync` and starved the notifier: every
   event flushed in one burst when the wait returned, which is why the F-296 run
   looked frozen.)

   `--wait` on the helper is the **headless fallback** (no plugin watching, e.g.
   a bare CI shell). It blocks the calling shell for the entire run:

   ```bash
   # headless only — from an agent `shell` call this holds the tool for the whole
   # matrix and leaves the transcript blind (the F-296 resume did exactly this).
   scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/run-detached.sh --flows all --reuse-session --wait
   ```

   Because that foot-gun recurs, `run-detached.sh` prints a loud warning before
   blocking. From an agent session: launch detached, then either let the plugin
   push, or call the `wait` tool — never `--wait`.

2. **`--reuse-session`** reuses the device session and signs in only when there
   is none, batching consecutive same-actor, setup-free journeys into one
   `maestro test` invocation (fewer JVMs). The shared
   `flows/_shared/session.yaml` subflow **never `clearState`s** — it launches
   without clearing, signs the current actor out when the journey's `actor:`
   (in `flows/matrix.yaml`) changes (`MOBILE_E2E_SWITCH=1`), and signs in as the
   target actor.    This is the single biggest wall-clock win. Omit it for a strict
   per-journey run (the default still switches session per flow, but no longer
   clears app data). The runner also **regroups the selected flows by actor**
   (firstLogin first, then each actor's standalone setup/oracle/`endsAs` flows
   before its setup-free run) so a batch is never interrupted by an unrelated
   flow. Alphabetical order otherwise scattered an actor's journeys among
   standalone flows — the F-296 run batched just 2 of 26 journeys (24
   invocations).

   **First login is one dedicated scenario.** The first-login walkthrough is
   gated on a per-member `AsyncStorage` flag, and `clearState` (`pm clear`)
   wipes it for *every* member. So exactly one journey declares
   `firstLogin: true` in `flows/matrix.yaml`: it is run **first** and alone, it
   is the only place that `clearState`s, and it asserts the fresh
   onboarding/walkthrough. Every other journey reuses a mixed set of sessions
   and never sees the walkthrough. Ordering the `clearState` first stops its
   app-data wipe from resetting the sessions the rest of the run depends on.
3. **Animations are disabled** for the run by `config.yaml`
   (`platform.android.disableAnimations: true` and
   `platform.ios.disableAnimations: true`, passed via `maestro test --config`),
   removing the per-command animation-settle wait on either platform. Override
   with `--config <file>`.
4. **`--no-seed`** runs `reset.js --no-seed` (mint actor auth, keep the seeded
   data) so a re-verification run skips the full DB seed.
5. **`--failed`** re-runs only the journeys that failed last time, from
   `.serve/mobile-e2e-last-run.json` (written after every run). Iterate on the
   failing subset, then do one full pass at the end.
6. **`--max-same-reason`** (default 3) is the fail-fast stop. Leave the default
   for a verification run so a systemic break stops early; pass `0` only for a
   full attribution sweep that must touch every journey.
7. The Maestro driver APKs are **not reinstalled** per invocation
   (`--no-reinstall-driver`); pass `--reinstall-driver` only if the driver is
   suspect.
8. **Setup batching (opt-in).** A journey that declares an additive `setup:` may
   add `batchSetup: true` in `matrix.yaml` so the runner runs its setup before a
   shared warm invocation instead of forcing a standalone one. It is refused
   (and the journey stays standalone) if its setup clears app data (`pm clear`/
   `clearState`), declares an `oracle:`, is `firstLogin:`, or changes actor
   (`endsAs`). Off by default: only opt in after a device run confirms the
   setups are order-independent.
9. **Scroll visibility.** `scrollUntilVisible` defaults to 100 % visibility,
   which flakes on a bottom-edge element (the `book-detail`
   `book-remove-arm` false negative: the node *was* on screen). The flows set
   `visibilityPercentage: 50` so a partially-scrolled target is accepted.
   When a target's position varies with content height (the same
   `book-remove-arm` is sometimes already on-screen and sometimes below the
   fold), guard the scroll with `runFlow: when: notVisible:` so the swipe runs
   only when the target is genuinely off-screen — a no-op swipe on an
   already-visible bottom-edge row can graze the tab bar and flake the step
   (F-313).

Project-specific defaults (app id, default actor/AVD, the dev-server and
optional backend-build commands) live in `scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/local.json` —
project-owned, not overwritten by the harness. The mechanism (`run-maestro.js`,
`check-flows.js`, `config.yaml`, `boot-emulator.sh`, `device-up.sh`,
`ios-simulator-up.sh`, `ios-simulator-down.sh`, `backend-build-cache.js`,
`run-detached.sh`, `job-events.js`) plus the
`job-notify` plugin are harness-owned under `templates/`, so fix them upstream
and `agent-harness update` the projects.

## Reuse vs. stop

- **Reuse** the emulator across runs *within a session* — leave it booted
  between tiers so a cold boot is not paid twice. Never kill an emulator you
  didn't start.
- **Stop the emulator at session end**, and a dev server as soon as its tier is
  done: `node scripts/serve.js stop --name <label>` (or `stop-all`). An idle
  emulator left up for hours held ~3 GB and was a direct contributor to the
  2026-09-29 freeze. You do not have to remember: `serve.js` records the owning
  session and **auto-closes** the serve — `reap` stops one whose owner's lease is
  gone/stale (or an untagged one past `idle_reap_minutes` with no recent log
  activity) and reconciles an untracked `agent-serve-*` unit from a killed
  session. `reap` runs at every `start` and when the context-guard plugin sees
  `session.deleted`, so an abandoned emulator/dev server is not kept alive.
- `node scripts/serve.js list` is the machine view: capacity (free RAM / swap /
  load / live serves) plus each process's age and whether it is heavy. Treat an
  old process as an idle-reap candidate; `npm run test:capacity` fails when the
  envelope is already exceeded.

## Diagnosing a failed step (UI hierarchy dump)

When a Maestro step fails (`Element not found`, `assertVisible …`), the fix starts
from the hierarchy the app actually rendered — which testIDs, text, and bounds
were on screen. Read it with the sanctioned probe, **not** a hand-rolled
`adb … uiautomator dump` / `python3` over `~/.maestro` (those trip the capacity
and tool guards, and were the F-311 dead end):

```bash
# Live: dump the current on-device hierarchy (lightweight; safe while the tier is up)
node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/ui-dump.js --live
node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/ui-dump.js --live --filter 'confirm-add|search-result'   # narrow the tree

# Offline: read Maestro's saved failure hierarchy (newest run by default)
node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/ui-dump.js --latest
node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/ui-dump.js --latest --flow scan-add --step step-063
node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/ui-dump.js --file ~/.maestro/tests/<run>/<flow>/screen-hierarchy/<step>.json

# Never `ls ~/.maestro` by hand — list the artifacts (hierarchy + screenshots):
node scripts/qa/mobile-e2e/ui-dump.js --list-artifacts --flow scan-add
```

`--json` emits the normalized tree for programmatic diffing. The probe launches
nothing heavy and is never gated by the capacity guard; it normalizes both a live
UIAutomator XML dump and Maestro's `screen-hierarchy/*.json` to the same shape
(`id | text | desc | class | bounds`).

## Anti-pattern that hangs the agent

```bash
# DO NOT DO THIS
setsid bash -c '~/android-sdk/emulator/emulator -avd <avd> … > /tmp/emulator.log 2>&1' < /dev/null &
```

The redirect lands on the **inner** command, not on the detached `bash -c`
wrapper. The wrapper therefore keeps the agent tool's stdout/stderr socket open
and stays alive as the emulator's parent — so the launch call never sees EOF and
subtly "runs" forever. No timeout fires, because the launched shell itself
already exited; the agent is simply blocked. The same failure hits a plain
trailing `&` (the process tree stays attached to the tool's console).

If you must launch by hand, redirect the wrapper's own fds:

```bash
setsid sh -c 'exec ~/android-sdk/emulator/emulator -avd <avd> …' </dev/null >/tmp/emulator.log 2>&1 &
```

## Recovering an already-wedged run

1. Interrupt the hung tool call in the agent (or restart the session).
2. **Keep the emulator** — it booted fine; verify with `adb devices` and
   `adb shell getprop sys.boot_completed`. Do not reboot it.
3. If the detached wrapper still lingers, confirm ownership before killing it:
   `node scripts/serve.js list` and check the PID's session/parent. Never kill an
   emulator you didn't start.
4. Relaunch through `serve.js` per this runbook before continuing.

See also: [wsl-optimizations.md](wsl-optimizations.md) (why WSL2 is the primary
environment) and `.agents/skills/mobile-engineer/SKILL.md` (the persona's device
rules).

# Nightly E2E cycle

How the harness tests the day's landed code off-hours, and closes the loop on a
fix. The day loop lands features on **cheap gates**; the expensive device/Maestro
tier is deliberately not run during the day. `scripts/nightly.js` runs the full
battery overnight against a dedicated `nightly` worktree fast-forwarded to
`origin/main`, writes a report, and reconciles the backlog.

```
DAY    worktree → cheap gates → land on main → CI → UAT deploy
       (no emulator / Maestro unless the user explicitly asks)
NIGHT  local timer (device matrix)  +  cloud workflow (unit/API/routes/browser)
       → report → board reconciliation
MORNING `orient` shows the verdict; reopened + new rows are waiting
```

## Two halves

- **Local (heavy, host-bound)** — `scripts/nightly.js` on a systemd `--user`
  timer. Runs the Android device/Maestro matrix (it needs the local emulator +
  GPU), plus the project's tiers, in a `nightly` worktree. Install with
  `agent-harness install-nightly --target .` (or `bash scripts/setup-nightly.sh install`).
- **Cloud (host-independent)** — `.github/workflows/nightly.yml`: unit, DB/API,
  route, and browser tiers on a schedule. Fails loudly (the red run is the alert).

## Config — `.agents/nightly.json` (project-owned)

Seeded create-if-missing by `init`/`update`; never overwritten on deploy.

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `worktree` | nightly worktree path (default `<repo>/../.worktrees/<repo>/nightly`) |
| `seedCmd` | optional dev-DB seed run before the phases (development only) |
| `waitForQuietMin` | wait this long for live human sessions to end before starting |
| `stalePendingNights` | nights a `nightly:pending` row may stay unvalidated before it is flagged |
| `keepDays` | report retention under `.agents/qa-runs/nightly/` |
| `fileBacklog` | reconcile the board (`add`/`reopen`/`validate`); default `true` |
| `notify` | optional command run with the report path on completion |
| `phases[]` | ordered battery: `{name, kind, script|cmd, heavy, timeoutMin}` |

Phase `kind`s: `gate` (a package.json script; a missing one is **skipped**, never
failed), `cmd` (a shell command), `device-e2e` (the built-in
device-up → Maestro matrix → device-down sequence, included only when the tier is
present). `heavy` phases run capped through `serve.js run`.

## The bug lifecycle

A nightly failure and its fix move through the board as **one row**:

```
NIGHT N   journey J fails, no row exists
          → backlog add "[nightly:flow=J] J e2e failed"
DAY N+1   you fix J on the cheap gates (NO Maestro), finalize as usual
NIGHT N+1 reconcile (journey-level):
          J passes          → archive <id> --closed "nightly-validated <date> <report>"
          J still fails      → backlog reopen <id> --reason "nightly <date>: still failing"
          a different journey→ backlog add (a new row)
```

- The marker `[nightly:flow=<journey>]` lives in the **Task cell**, which every
  board section preserves, so the row stays on the radar through
  Open → In progress → Archive without any schema change.
- Matching is **journey-level**: one row per broken journey, reopened until
  green. A signature change on the same journey is recorded in the reopen reason
  but still reopens the same row (the fix was incomplete/regressed); a different
  journey's failure is a new row.
- **No Maestro during the day.** A device-only path is addressed in the QA plan
  as `audited: device tier deferred to nightly [nightly:flow=<journey>]` (a valid
  `audited:`/`waived:` reason). `finalize`/`ship` never demand the device tier.
- Repeated reopens escalate P2 → P1 (`[nightly:reopen=N]`); stale pending rows
  surface in `orient` and `agent-harness doctor`.

## Running and reading

```bash
npm run nightly -- run            # run the cycle now (foreground)
npm run nightly -- run --dry-run  # phase plan, no side effects
node scripts/nightly.js report    # last verdict + failures + board actions
node scripts/nightly.js status    # last run + rows awaiting validation
```
